lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s paperwork ordeal
lead.head: Prove you exist. Again. Every year

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 74

body: Amit Varma opened the episode by doubt­ing that his co-host was his co-host. “Bearded econ­o­mists look alike to me,” he said. “Prove to me that you’re Ajay Shah. Kaagaz dikhaao!” {074-J01}
Shah had no pa­pers and of­fered his face in­stead. The joke set up an episode on KYC, the know-your-customer checks Indian banks keep run­ning.
Shah’s own bank asks him every year to prove again that he is who he said he was. Accounts with money in them, he said, get frozen when KYC goes wrong.
For the priv­i­leged, who can march up to the bank man­ager, it is a nui­sance. For most Indians, Shah said, “this is just a liv­ing night­mare”.
## Privacy is pri­vacy
Shah began with first prin­ci­ples. A spy who fol­lows a per­son learns what she says, does and buys; a com­plete view of her fi­nances, he ar­gued, re­veals as much.
The propo­si­tion, he said, was sim­ple: “if you be­lieve in per­sonal pri­vacy, you should equally be­lieve in fi­nan­cial pri­vacy.” {074-C01}

The re­tort “if you have noth­ing to hide” misses the point. People who know they are watched bend their be­hav­iour to suit the watcher. “A world in which you do not have pri­vacy is not free­dom,” Shah said.

His model is the wire­tap. In lib­eral democ­ra­cies a po­lice of­fi­cer must con­vince a judge with prima facie ev­i­dence, the tap lasts a fi­nite time, and no­body runs mass sur­veil­lance of everyone’s phone.

Shah wants the same for money: cus­tomers able to tell their bank to delete trans­ac­tions after three days, and po­lice need­ing a war­rant to watch a sus­pect for a fixed pe­riod. “It is only in a po­lice state that a policeman’s job is easy,” he said. {074-C04}
## A slow creep

The his­tory, as Shah told it, is a slow creep. In 1933 Nazi Germany made its cit­i­zens dis­close their over­seas as­sets. In the 1970s American banks had to re­port large trans­ac­tions to the tax au­thor­i­ties, and no­body ob­jected, be­cause it was only about tax evaders.
Richard Nixon’s war on drugs cre­ated the crime of money laun­der­ing, and a club of coun­tries, FATF, grew around it. After the 9/11 at­tacks the US Treasury pushed its rules on the world.
## The world’s worst

Shah dis­agrees with the FATF rules even in rich coun­tries, but in London, Zurich or Washington open­ing a bank ac­count in­volves lit­tle mis­ery. In India each layer makes them worse: the government’s rules, then the RBI, then the bank, then the front­line em­ployee.
No one an­swers for the wel­fare of cit­i­zens. Each, Shah said, is think­ing: “My only ob­jec­tive is to cover my ass.” {074-C10}
The poor and small firms give up and fall back on cash, gold and real es­tate.
Shah also con­fessed that he had once be­lieved Aadhaar would fix all this. “And in hind­sight I re­al­ize how wrong it was,” he said. {074-S07}
The first Aadhaar num­ber was is­sued in 2009, yet banks still de­mand fresh KYC every year. “CPUs are never the an­swer,” Shah said.

His larger les­son was to be scep­ti­cal of “global best prac­tice”. Policies that seem to work in America rest there on in­vis­i­ble sup­ports: lib­eral democ­racy, courts, checks and bal­ances, norms. It was “stupid in India to ac­cept this”, he said.
Varma’s song of the day was *Every Breath You Take* by The Police. Shah’s ad­vice: “Please email this to all the civil ser­vants in your life.”

second.label: Terror finance
second.head: The 555 loophole
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why following the money after 9/11 never stopped terror plots

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the cigarette box of diamonds

body: After the 9/11 at­tacks, the idea took hold that ter­ror plots could be caught by find­ing the $100,000 wired by a Pakistani major gen­eral to Mohammed Atta, who or­gan­ised the at­tacks. Ajay Shah called it “not a very bright idea”.

His coun­terex­am­ple is a 555 cig­a­rette box packed with di­a­monds, which holds about $100,000 and is in­vis­i­ble to X-ray ma­chines. {074-C07} He won­dered aloud how mod­ern ma­chines would see it. Monitor seven bil­lion peo­ple, he said, and ter­ror­ists sim­ply move to other chan­nels. {#sevenbillion}
By now, Shah said, it is well known that the sys­tem has not dis­rupted ter­ror plots. It has only fouled up fi­nance and given gov­ern­ments more in­for­ma­tion about their sub­jects.

quote.text: You want to move a hun­dred thou­sand dol­lars to Mohammed Atta, you just have to carry one cig­a­rette case.

third.head: Cruelty by paperwork

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the paperwork maze

body: A very smart friend of Amit Varma’s, in her 40s, had a sup­ple­men­tary credit card linked to her husband’s. She had done her KYC the year be­fore, but this year she could not get through the pa­per­work in time. She lost the card; he kept his. {074-S03}
Varma also re­mem­bered his fa­ther in his last years, un­able to cope. “It was cru­elty,” he said, “to ex­pect a man of ad­vanc­ing years or a woman of ad­vanc­ing years to deal with all of this.”
Even Harsh Vardhan, a se­nior bank­ing fig­ure who knows the peo­ple who run the banks, told Varma what a night­mare his own KYC had been: phone calls here, phone calls there. {074-S02}
Poor peo­ple and small firms, Ajay Shah said, “just look at all this and they give up”.

p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case for financial privacy, and how India came to have the world’s worst KYC

quote.text: Then if you will shat­ter fi­nan­cial pri­vacy, you have shat­tered right to as­so­ci­a­tion.

box.title: The thinker behind the episode
box.text: Ajay Shah said this episode was built with the in­tel­lec­tual guid­ance and sup­port of Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah, whom Amit Varma called “a very fine thinker” and who has been a guest on his pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*. {#bhargavi}

sections.label: The first principle
sections.head: Your wallet is your diary
sections.caption: financial privacy as personal privacy
body: Ajay Shah went back to fun­da­men­tals: what is the case for fi­nan­cial pri­vacy? A spy who fol­lows a per­son learns what she says, does and buys, and in a lib­eral democ­racy that is not on. A full pic­ture of her fi­nances, he ar­gued, re­veals as much. {074-C01}

The reply “if you have noth­ing to hide” misses the point. Once you know you are being ob­served, Shah said, you are in the panop­ti­con, and your days are dis­torted “out of def­er­ence to the watcher”. {#chillingeffect}
Amit Varma chal­lenged any­one who uses that ar­gu­ment to make their Google searches pub­lic. {#incognito} “What do you do in the Chrome incog­nito win­dow?” he asked.
## Firms and fun­ders

Shah ex­tended the case to com­pa­nies. Populism, he said, grants in­di­vid­u­als some pri­vacy but treats firms as fair game. Yet a firm’s cus­tomers and ven­dors can be read from its fi­nan­cial state­ments, and that list in hos­tile hands could de­stroy it. {074-C02}

Privacy also un­der­pins free­dom of as­so­ci­a­tion, the right to form clubs, par­ties, NGOs and com­pa­nies. If the state can see who funds an or­gan­i­sa­tion, the pow­er­ful can go after its fun­ders. {074-C03} Varma’s ex­am­ple: a rul­ing party could order a tax raid on some­one do­nat­ing to the op­po­si­tion.

~ Varma, draw­ing on his con­ver­sa­tion with Rahul Matthan, added that pri­vacy is a his­tor­i­cal achieve­ment. Thicker walls and sep­a­rate bed­rooms gave peo­ple the soli­tude in which a rich in­te­rior life could grow.

quote.text: Then if you will shat­ter fi­nan­cial pri­vacy, you have shat­tered right to as­so­ci­a­tion.

sections.label: The backstory
sections.head: A Nazi idea goes global
sections.caption: the history of financial surveillance
body: Banks once kept their customers’ af­fairs pri­vate by an in­for­mal code, Ajay Shah said. The break came in 1933, when Nazi Germany re­quired every cit­i­zen to dis­close their over­seas as­sets. Governments all over the world now do the same. “We have nor­mal­ized op­pres­sion in the mod­ern world,” he said. {074-C06}

The American creep began with the tax au­thor­i­ties. In the 1970s banks had to re­port trans­ac­tions above ten thou­sand dol­lars to the IRS, and no­body spoke up, be­cause it was only about tax evaders. {#tenthousand}

Richard Nixon’s war on drugs then cre­ated the crime of money laun­der­ing, and the Financial Action Task Force grew around it. The US law, Shah said, was called the Banking Privacy Act: “It is ac­tu­ally the de­struc­tion of pri­vacy in Banking Act.” {#orwell}
## Join, or else
FATF is a closed club of major coun­tries, and India, Shah said, was its last mem­ber. Others faced a choice: sign up to fi­nan­cial sur­veil­lance or face more fric­tion in the world. {074-R19}
After the 9/11 at­tacks, the US Treasury cham­pi­oned AML-CFT, anti-money laun­der­ing and coun­ter­ing the fi­nanc­ing of ter­ror, across the world.
~ By now, Shah said, it is well known that none of this has dis­rupted ter­ror plots. It has fouled up fi­nance and handed gov­ern­ments more in­for­ma­tion about their sub­jects.

quote.text: And the slip­pery slope began. And then it started get­ting worse and it started get­ting worse.

sections.label: India’s version
sections.head: Worse, worse, worst
sections.caption: why India’s KYC is the worst
body: Ajay Shah dis­agrees with the FATF rules even in rich coun­tries. But open a bank ac­count in London, Zurich or Washington, he said, and your level of mis­ery is low, like an air­port check that “may be stupid, but it’s not so bad”. {#londonzurich}

In India the same rules pass through layer after layer. The gov­ern­ment writes their harsh­est ver­sion into its rules. The RBI, Shah said, “will make some­thing worse out of it”. {#rbi} The bank does the same, and the front­line em­ployee in­ter­prets it in the worst pos­si­ble way.
No one at any step an­swers for the wel­fare of cit­i­zens. Each, in Shah’s telling, is think­ing: “My only ob­jec­tive is to cover my ass.” {074-C10}
## The cost
The heav­i­est bur­den falls on the poor, who lack the time and the abil­ity to fight through the com­plex­ity. Poor peo­ple and small firms give up, and fi­nan­cial ex­clu­sion fol­lows.
It has be­come harder and harder, Shah said, to run a firm of five, ten, twenty or forty peo­ple in India. {#smallfirms}
~ Meanwhile, he said, “all of us just roll our eyes and get mis­er­able and put up one sen­tence on Twitter and let it go”.

quote.text: So each one comes up with a harder and cra­zier ver­sion of it.

sections.label: The mea culpa
sections.head: Chips won’t fix the state
sections.caption: why Aadhaar didn’t end KYC
body: Ajay Shah owned up to an error. People in fi­nance, him­self in­cluded, had thought Aadhaar would pro­vide an end run around the KYC mess. “I am guilty,” he said. “I’m part of this thought process.” {074-S07}

Aadhaar was sup­posed to make the prob­lem mys­te­ri­ously van­ish, he said, be­cause his iris scan does not change through his life. Yet the first Aadhaar num­ber was given out in 2009, and in 2024 his bank still tells him to do his KYC afresh every year. {#aadhaar2009}
His gen­eral law: “Adding CPUs to a mal­func­tion­ing Indian gov­ern­ment never makes the Indian gov­ern­ment bet­ter.” {074-C11} You have to go deep in­side, he said, and fix the or­gan­i­sa­tion.
## The per­fect and the good

Amit Varma, not want­ing the per­fect to be the enemy of the good, asked why a sim­ple cen­tral di­rec­tive could not de­clare that Aadhaar suf­fices. Shah an­swered with pub­lic choice the­ory. Officials who want to cover them­selves will keep com­ing up with one more rule, so “the idea that good sense will pre­vail is the flaw”.
~ The fix, he said, lies at the root cause, in “the hard work of hu­man­i­ties and lib­eral arts”. {#humanities}

quote.text: So try­ing to find an end run around prob­lems of pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion with a tech­no­log­i­cal sil­ver bul­let, that is the core flaw.

sections.label: The lesson
sections.head: Handle imports with care
sections.caption: global best practice
body: What would a good fu­ture look like, Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah wants con­sti­tu­tional law and the courts to shut down all mass sur­veil­lance in fi­nance, build­ing on the Puttaswamy rul­ing and the right to as­so­ci­a­tion. {#courts}

A cus­tomer should be able to tell a bank to delete every trans­ac­tion “one mil­lisec­ond after they take place”. Police who have proved that some­one is a drug dealer should get a war­rant from some­thing like an American FISA court, and then see that person’s trans­ac­tions for 90 days. {#ninetydays}
## Invisible in­fra­struc­ture
The wider les­son, which Shah traced to Lant Pritchett and to Kelkar and Shah, is to be scep­ti­cal of “global best prac­tice”. {#pritchett}

A pol­icy that seems to work in the United States rests there on sup­ports no­body sees: lib­eral democ­racy, checks and bal­ances, courts, com­mu­ni­ties and norms. Naively trans­planted into India, Shah ar­gued, it does far worse. {074-C12}
~ It was “wrong and dan­ger­ous and evil”, he said, for the US Treasury to push fi­nan­cial sur­veil­lance all over the world, “and it was stupid in India to ac­cept this”.

quote.text: There is in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture in the form of lib­eral democ­racy, checks and bal­ances, courts, com­mu­ni­ties, norms.
But the point is that when we give those free­doms away, it af­fects our se­cu­rity against the state. Who’s gonna pro­tect us from the state? That is the dan­ger. So ac­tu­ally we lose both.

p3.title: Tales from the paper trail
p3.deck: A man declared dead, a gangster’s laundromats, Swiss secrets and a Russian surprise

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a man who had to prove he was alive
stories.head: Alive, but not on paper
body: Lal Bihari was born in 1951 in Azamgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Amit Varma said. In 1976 his cousins de­cided they wanted his land. Bribes were paid, a death cer­tifi­cate was pro­duced, and at 25 Lal Bihari found he was of­fi­cially dead.

If paper could make him dead, it could make him alive. He or­gan­ised his own fu­neral and ap­plied for com­pen­sa­tion for his al­leged widow. Then he threw stones at a po­lice sta­tion, hop­ing an ar­rest would prove he ex­isted.
The bribed po­lice, Varma said, “for the first time in recorded Indian his­tory” chose to “take a Gandhian view of the sit­u­a­tion and ig­nore the stones”. {074-J02}

Next he kid­napped a 10-year-old cousin, ex­pect­ing the fam­ily to come and set­tle mat­ters. “There are many kids in that fam­ily, no one gives a shit,” Varma said. After ten days Lal Bihari gave the boy ice cream and sent him home. {074-J03}

He stood against VP Singh in Allahabad in 1988 and Rajiv Gandhi in Amethi in 1989, since a can­di­date on the rolls must be alive. He re­named him­self Lal Bihari Mritak, mri­tak mean­ing dead, and founded the Uttar Pradesh Mritak Sangh. It grew to twenty thou­sand mem­bers, all de­clared dead. {#twentythousand}
In 1994 he was de­clared alive again. How many of the twenty thou­sand made it back? “Four peo­ple,” came the an­swer. “That’s how hard it is.” {#fourpeople}
~ We all strug­gle to come to terms with our mor­tal­ity, Varma said. “But imag­ine com­ing to terms with your own death, which has al­legedly al­ready hap­pened and you’re still alive.” {074-S01}
stories.why: Once the state’s paper ver­sion of a per­son parts from the real one, the paper wins. Four out of twenty thou­sand is how hard a bu­reau­cratic record is to re­verse, and it is the frame the hosts set for their talk on KYC.
stories.postscript: Behind every in­de­pen­dent can­di­date who loses a de­posit, Varma said, there is a story “rich in cin­e­matic po­ten­tial”. {074-J04}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the man declared dead

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why Swiss bank secrecy began
stories.head: Banking on discretion
body: Banks had al­ways kept their customers’ af­fairs pri­vate as an in­for­mal norm, Ajay Shah said. Then in 1933 Hitler came to power, and Nazi Germany de­manded that every cit­i­zen dis­close their over­seas as­sets. No state had done that be­fore.

Switzerland, then the bank­ing cap­i­tal of the world, feared that in­for­mal codes would not pro­tect its for­eign cus­tomers. So it passed the first laws say­ing that no bank would di­vulge in­for­ma­tion about its cus­tomers ex­cept on the order of a Swiss judge. {#swissjudge}
A German pros­e­cu­tor pur­su­ing a crime in Germany would be dis­re­garded. “We don’t care,” Shah said, speak­ing for the Swiss.

~ Shah dis­misses the pop­ulist noise about Swiss banks and tax havens. In the 20th cen­tury peo­ple fled their gov­ern­ments, he said, and a Swiss bank was one way to pro­tect their wealth and pri­vate lives. {074-S05}

quote.text: To un­der­stand the 20th cen­tury is to see that these are the ways by which peo­ple pro­tected them­selves against gov­ern­ments.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Swiss bank secrecy

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on where a crime got its name
stories.head: Dirty money, clean shirts
body: In 1930s America, Ajay Shah re­called, the gang­ster Al Capone had a con­cept for his crim­i­nal cash: take it into a busi­ness with cash in­come, namely laun­dro­mats.

Laundromats are shops where you take your pile of clothes, stick them into a ma­chine and col­lect them washed. Capone’s il­licit cash was shown as the laundromat’s in­come. “And that’s how the word money laun­der­ing emerged,” Shah said. {074-S04}
“We are all in this mess,” Shah said, “be­cause gov­ern­ments want to go block this kind of money laun­der­ing.” From that ef­fort grew a world­wide sys­tem of fi­nan­cial sur­veil­lance.
~ Every time the Enforcement Directorate ap­pears in the news­pa­pers, Shah said, this is the prob­lem at work. {#edpapers}
stories.why: The crime that now jus­ti­fies watch­ing everyone’s money began as one gangster’s cover story. In Shah’s telling, every Enforcement Directorate head­line is a con­se­quence of states try­ing to block that trick.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Al Capone’s laundromats

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an official’s talk with Russian counterparts
stories.head: From Washington, with lessons
body: A good friend of Ajay Shah’s, an Indian of­fi­cial, once had pri­vate, quiet con­ver­sa­tions with Russian coun­ter­parts. They told him some­thing, Shah said, with a great sense of won­der.
“Did you know the American Treasury is teach­ing us how to op­press our own peo­ple?” {074-S06}
The US Treasury, Shah ex­plained, had taught the Russian gov­ern­ment how to build a mass sur­veil­lance sys­tem in fi­nance. The Russians, he said, had not known how to do it by them­selves.

~ For Shah, this was where the American push against money laun­der­ing and ter­ror fi­nance after the 9/11 at­tacks had led. The whole story, he said, “is re­ally a blot” on the con­science of the United States. {#blot}
stories.why: Tools built against ter­ror can be turned on cit­i­zens. A sys­tem made in the name of fol­low­ing terrorists’ money, Shah ar­gued, handed the Russian gov­ern­ment the know-how to watch its own peo­ple.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 74. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Al Capone (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Richard Nixon (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Satyajit Ray (Dinu Alam Newyork, CC BY-SA 4.0); Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck (Deutsches Filmmuseum, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Every Breath You Take
shelf.creator: The Police
shelf.why: Its re­frain, ‘I’ll be watch­ing you’, fits a state that watches every trans­ac­tion.

shelf.title: The Lives of Others
shelf.creator: Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck
shelf.why: A debut film about sur­veil­lance in di­vided Germany, about watch­ing and being watched and how that changes both sides; Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece and one of the finest debut films he has seen.

shelf.title: Pather Panchali
shelf.creator: Satyajit Ray
shelf.why: Amit puts it among the great­est debut films ever made.

shelf.title: Court
shelf.creator: Chaitanya Tamhane
shelf.why: Another debut film Amit places at the very top.

shelf.title: Chicago PD
shelf.why: He says it started off mid­dling and be­came re­ally good in later sea­sons.

shelf.title: The Baptist, the Bootlegger and the Dead Man Walking
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ten ac­count of the Lal Bihari saga, which ap­plies the boot­leg­gers-and-Baptists frame­work.

shelf.title: The Bankable Wisdom of Harsh Vardhan (Episode 352 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Harsh Vardhan, whom Ajay calls a deep thinker on banks, ar­gues that bank­ing, mag­i­cal and fun­da­men­tally frag­ile, is es­sen­tial to a suc­cess­ful cap­i­tal­ism.

shelf.title: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah Will Not Wear a Blue Tie to Work (Episode 389 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah on fi­nan­cial pri­vacy and the in­side story of how an­a­lysts and wonks came to­gether to draft India’s bank­ruptcy code, which Amit calls ab­so­lutely in­spir­ing.

shelf.title: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (Episode 360 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Rahul Matthan makes the strong­est case that Aadhaar has pri­vacy built into its de­sign, the view Ajay chal­lenges.

shelf.title: Privacy 3.0
shelf.creator: Rahul Matthan
shelf.why: A book-length treat­ment of the pri­vacy ideas Amit draws on in this episode.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: Analysing India’s KYC Framework through the Privacy Lens
shelf.creator: Vrinda Bhandari, Rishab Bailey & Trishee Goyal
shelf.why: Looks at Indian KYC through the pri­vacy lens that Ajay ar­gues should be the start­ing point.

shelf.title: Analysing India’s KYC Framework: Can We Do Things Better?
shelf.creator: Rishab Bailey, Trishee Goyal, Renuka Sane & Ridhi Varma
shelf.why: Asks the con­struc­tive ques­tion the episode ends on: what would a bet­ter KYC frame­work look like?

shelf.title: Don’t Follow the Money
shelf.creator: Peter R Neumann
shelf.why: Fits his ar­gu­ment that track­ing money has not dis­rupted ter­ror­ist plots and has only fouled up fi­nance.

shelf.title: Identifying the Real SBO: A critique of the LinkedIn and Samsung Orders
shelf.creator: Chirag Motwani & Ananya Badaga
shelf.why: Further read­ing on India’s dis­clo­sure de­mands on firms, con­nected to his ar­gu­ment that firms de­serve fi­nan­cial pri­vacy.

shelf.title: Power and Discourse in Policy Diffusion: Anti-Money Laundering in Developing States
shelf.creator: JC Sharman
shelf.why: About how anti-money-laundering rules spread to de­vel­op­ing coun­tries, which is the theme of his ‘don’t take blindly from the USA’ ar­gu­ment.

laughs.text: The cold open is a KYC check on the co-host. Amit: “I’m not sure if this is my good friend Ajay. Bearded econ­o­mists look alike to me. Are you Ajay Shah? Prove to me that you’re Ajay Shah. Kaagaz dikhaao!” Ajay: “I don’t have pa­pers. Will you rec­og­nize my face? FRT, face recog­ni­tion tech­nol­ogy.” Amit: “Biometrics. Take off your glasses, I’ll scan your eyes.” Amit then in­tro­duces him­self as “Amit al­legedly”.
Amit on the po­lice fac­ing Lal Bihari’s stones: “the po­lice, for the first time in recorded Indian his­tory, take a Gandhian view of the sit­u­a­tion and ig­nore the stones.”
On Lal Bihari’s failed kid­nap­ping: “India’s pop­u­la­tion is awe­some. There are many kids in that fam­ily, no one gives a shit.” After ten days he gives the boy ice cream and sends him home.

A run­ning gag casts the episode’s cam­era­man Vaishnav Vyas as Lal Bihari in the film ver­sion. Amit says be­hind every in­de­pen­dent can­di­date who loses a de­posit there is a story “rich in life, rich in drama, rich in pathos. Rich in cin­e­matic po­ten­tial. Are you lis­ten­ing, Vaishnav Vyas?”
Ajay on why his bank wants yearly re-KYC: “Like proofs have the de­pre­ci­a­tion and they van­ish with time, so it has to be re-upped.”
Amit on a re­ported plot to hide bombs in breast im­plants: “You’re not gonna say take out your breast im­plants and put them on the se­cu­rity tray.”

Ajay sings The Police: “Every vow you break, every claim you stake, I’ll be watch­ing you. This has been tra­di­tion­ally thought of as a creepy male stalker song, but gen­tle read­ers, please email this to all the civil ser­vants in your life.” Amit: “The state is a creepy male stalker. And much worse.”
Amit, after say­ing The Lives of Others shows how watch­ing can change both watcher and watched: “So I don’t think the Indian state is re­ally going to get re­formed be­cause they’re watch­ing us.”
Yes Minister’s po­lit­i­cal logic, quoted by Amit as the state’s re­flex after a ter­ror at­tack: “we must do some­thing, this is some­thing, let’s do it.”
Bruce Schneier’s term “se­cu­rity the­ater”: se­cu­rity that is per­formed rather than real.
Ajay quotes “the great man” on lib­erty and safety, with the terms swapped: “those who will sac­ri­fice se­cu­rity in ex­change for free­dom will end up with nei­ther se­cu­rity nor free­dom.”

“That old saw of power cor­rupts, ab­so­lute power cor­rupts ab­so­lutely”, in­voked by Amit to ex­plain what a state does with sur­veil­lance power: crack down on dis­sent and po­lit­i­cal op­po­nents.
